news.title: Haley Stevens urges El-Sayed to ditch Hasan Piker affiliation after Michigan primary
news.text: Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., urged Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated her in Michigan's fierce Democratic primary election, to sever ties with controversial, far-left streamer Hasan Piker on "The Sunday Briefing," saying the party's nominee should now turn his attention toward Michigan voters as he pivots to the general election. Stevens maintained her primary-season criticism of Piker even while backing El-Sayed, describing herself as still committed to the party. "It certainly makes sense to get rid of this Hasan Piker affiliation," she said, also asserting that the Democratic plans for healthcare, democracy and Black-owned businesses are better than those of Republican Mike Rogers, who will oppose El-Sayed in the Senate race. Asked whether El-Sayed had said or done anything other than winning the Democratic nomination to earn the support and assuage the concerns of groups that voted for Stevens, such as Jewish voters, Black voters or Reagan-era Democrats, Stevens pointed to her own good performance with those demographics, identifying herself as a Zionist Democrat and asserting that her party had room for all those communities. news.title: Most voters say they are worse off under Trump, new poll says
news.text:
Americans broadly believe that the economy is growing worse under President Donald Trump’s stewardship and say that they are personally worse off after a year and a half of his second presidency.

The findings are part of a poll conducted by Focaldata for the Financial Times and gauged Americans’ mood about Republican control of Washington as the midterms rapidly approach.

Overall, Americans of all political stripes say that they are in a financially worse position than they were on January 19, 2025, when Joe Biden concluded his presidency and prepared to hand over the keys. Roughly 53 percent of all registered voters, including nearly 25 percent of Republicans, said they were in a worse position now, as the war with Iran and other issues continue to drive up consumer costs, including the price of fuel.

The poll also found a clear advantage for Democrats on a midterm generic ballot, with 51 percent of Americans saying they’d vote for a Democrat over a Republican in November’s midterm elections. 45 percent preferred the Republican.

It’s a plethora of warning signs for Trump and his party as they seek to hold on to majorities in both chambers of Congress this fall. On the issue of jobs and the economy, more voters said they trusted Democrats over Republicans — possibly the worst sign in the poll for the GOP, which credited support on those issues for Trump’s victory over Kamala Harris in 2024.

The president’s approval rating remains grim. The poll found 55 percent of Americans disapprove of the job he’s doing, and his support among Republicans is slowly beginning to crack. 

One in five now disapprove of his performance so far through his second term. His approval rating among Republicans dropped eight points between this latest poll, released Sunday, and the Financial Times’ previous survey in July.

Democrats need to pick up four seats in the Senate and the same number in the House to win double majorities in Congress next year. Doing so in either chamber would effectively put a stop to any partisan legislation for the next two years, effectively neutering the GOP’s agenda apart from what the president and his Cabinet secretaries can achieve at the executive level.

The retaking of both chambers even theoretically opens the door to the possibility of a third round of impeachment proceedings, but Democratic leaders have backed away from such inclinations in public statements and interviews as the midterms approach.

More likely is the prospect of Democrats seeking to expose the administration to political damage through congressional investigations if they retake the House or Senate. Democrats have already pledged to investigate the Trump family’s financial dealings, which have included record-setting profits under his second presidency. 

Several committees are also eyeing congressional subpoena power to investigate the firings and institutional changes wrought by Elon Musk’s DOGE initiative.

Republicans have endured the narrowest margins in the House for more than a year, leaving the chamber constantly at war with itself and making passage of the “One Big, Beautiful Bill” last year an arduous task. The president, his team and the GOP’s united refusal to negotiate with Democrats on its policy objectives have also forced the party to achieve most of its policy gains through the budget reconciliation package, which is limited to budget-related issues but allows the 60-vote filibuster threshold to be avoided.

Trump has pushed Republicans to scrap the filibuster and hurriedly pass other legislation, to no avail.

This latest Financial Times survey comes on the heels of a Reuters/Ipsos survey that found support for the U.S. war with Iran to be extremely low, with a wide majority of Americans believing that Trump had failed to lay out his goals or his strategy.

The Financial Times poll was conducted between August 7 to August 10 with a survey pool of 1,913 registered voters. The margin of error was 2.9 percentage points.
news.summary: One in five Republicans say their finances are worse after year and a half of Trump
news.author: John Bowden

news.title: Woke 2.0 Will Be Worse
news.text:
Readers familiar with Dr. Seuss’s classic, The Cat in the Hat, will remember the twin chaos agents Thing 1 and Thing 2. “‘These Things are good Things,’” the Cat reassures the children whose mother has inexplicably left them under the supervision of a fish. “‘They are tame. Oh, so tame! / They have come here to play.’” The Things briefly feign innocence, then quickly reveal themselves to be marauding imps, knocking over nightstands and ruining the linens. “I do not like the way that they play!” says the son of the house.

Now here comes Woke 1 and Woke 2. “Woke 1 was crazy,” said U.S. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, quoting an unnamed city councilman in a viral interview for ABC. The congresswoman sheepishly acknowledged that Americans did not like the way Woke 1 played out, while also implicitly announcing that there will soon be, or already is, a Woke 2. And it will be tame. Oh, so tame!

There is, in fact, a new version of wokeness in the making. But just as Thing 2 was fundamentally identical to Thing 1, Woke 2 will not be any different in essence from Woke 1. They are both here to upend the furniture. Wokeness in all its forms is grievance politics. Its central idea is that an injustice lies at the heart of America and must be corrected to atone for the historical misery inflicted on groups of innocents.

What is changing in Woke 2 is the account of who those innocents are, and how they have been wronged. Woke 1 was founded on the notion that black women are the most oppressed, and therefore most righteous, of all people. “I’m thinking,” said Kamala Harris in her vice presidential victory speech, “about the generations of women—black women.” She mentioned many other kinds of women, of course, but the list began and ended with “the black women—who are too often overlooked, but so often prove that they are the backbone of this country.”

news.title: What Bezos did at the Washington Post could happen in NZ
news.text:
Pro-Trump media ownership is influencing journalism in the US. Think it couldn’t happen here? Anna Fifield argues developments over the past year say otherwise.

The walls inside the Washington Post building on K Street – the flash new premises provided by Jeff Bezos after he bought the newspaper in 2013 – are covered with inspirational quotes.

There’s this one, from Ben Bradlee, the editor-in-chief at the time of the Watergate scandal: “The truth, no matter how bad, is never as dangerous as a lie in the long run.”

And this: “There is only one good reason to enter journalism: When we do our job we can make a difference.” That’s from Don Graham, scion of the family that owned the Post for 80 years before selling it to Bezos.

Whenever I went back to head office during my years as Tokyo then Beijing bureau chief, and most recently as Asia editor, I found them inspiring. This was my calling. It might sound trite (or self important) but to this day, I believe that a free and flourishing press is crucial to democracy. 

On my last visit to the mothership, however, I noticed that a new inscription had appeared on the walls. It was from Bezos and it said: “What’s dangerous is not to evolve.”

At the time, I snickered, but I shrugged it off as an owner’s right to install himself among these lions of journalism.

After all, he’d been a great owner for the first 11 years: He had invested heavily in the Post and backed the Star Wars-sounding motto, Democracy Dies in Darkness, but had not inserted himself into editorial operations. It seemed he was truly interested in journalism as a democratic institution, rather than pursuing the Post as a vanity project (after all, he had his space programme for that).

I should have seen that quote on the wall as a portent. Boy, did he evolve in his ownership of the Post – and in ways that would soon feel dangerous.

In the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, Bezos would spike the Post’s endorsement of Kamala Harris, a decision that saw the exodus of several hundred thousand subscribers and many brand-name, Pulitzer Prize-winning journalists. 

Then came the Amazon founder’s edict that the Post’s opinion page would henceforth be devoted to “personal liberties and free markets”.

Another exodus. A round of devastating buyouts.

Then came the biggest blow of all: Some 375 journalists – including me – were laid off in a single day in February this year. It was brutal. Almost everyone on the international desk – including the entire China, Middle East, Ukraine teams – gone. Sports, gone. Books, gone. The flagship Post Reports podcast, gone. The local, climate, photo, technology and video desks were left as shells of their former selves. Almost half the newsroom disappeared overnight.

Cost cutting was the ostensible reason — although the Post is owned by one of the world’s richest men.

This same trend is occurring across the United States. Billionaire David Ellison bought the CBS network and appointed Bari Weiss, a right-wing columnist with no television experience, as editor-in-chief. It’s been haemorrhaging viewers, as well as journalists, who are complaining about pro-Trump editorial interference.

Ellison has now set his sights on Warner Bros. Discovery, the owner of CNN, a well-established global channel that Trump regularly labels a “corrupt organisation” that he says is publishing “fake news”.

That would make the overall media eco-system friendlier to Trump and his “alternative facts”. And that’s without even mentioning the pro-Trump propaganda over at Fox News, the president’s preferred TV channel, and the substantial reach he has with his all-caps, late-night blast medium, Truth Social.

It’s easy to look at what’s happening in the US as an aberration in their system, the result of an increasingly authoritarian president going unchecked by a cowed Congress. But we shouldn’t be too blasé. This past year has seen some worrying developments in New Zealand involving a seemingly politically-driven billionaire seeking media influence and a government that looked like it was attempting to intimidate media figures.

Canadian-born private equity billionaire Jim Grenon, a New Zealand resident who has backed anti-vax conspiracy theorists, is now the largest shareholder of NZME, owner of the New Zealand Herald and Newstalk ZB, and is a director on its board.

He may have failed in his board takeover attempt – at least for now – but he has continued to use his financial resources to fund challenges to other reporting he dislikes. 

He funded a defamation case taken by Julian Batchelor, the conspiracy theorist and organiser of the “Stop Co-Governance” roadshow, against TVNZ and disinformation expert Sanjana Hattotuwa – and tried to keep his involvement secret. In both cases, Grenon tried to shape NZ media and public discourse from behind the scenes, which is precisely what worried NZME’s board and shareholder groups from the outset.

Then there’s concerns about government attempts at interference.

Act leader and deputy prime minister David Seymour – who is also a shareholding minister for both RNZ and TVNZ – earlier this year sharply criticised the management of both state broadcasters.

Seymour attacked RNZ’s decision to appoint John Campbell as co-host of Morning Report, saying opinion pieces Campbell wrote while working for TVNZ should have put the idea of him hosting the flagship programme “out of the question”. Referring to RNZ chief executive Paul Thompson, Seymour said “that guy’s got an awful lot to answer for, and I suspect that he won’t be answering the call at RNZ for much longer”.

RNZ chairman Jim Mather strongly defended RNZ and its management, saying it is editorially independent, and indeed, legislation prohibits ministers from interfering in editorial decisions at RNZ or TVNZ. Seymour denies he stepped outside the bounds of law.

Fast forward, and Thompson has announced he’ll leave his position at the end of the year – a decision he said he made at the end of 2025, before Seymour weighed in – while Mather’s term came to an end last month.

Paul Goldsmith, the minister for media and communications, distanced himself from Seymour’s remarks, but has – at the same time – proposed changes that have also raised concerns about the erosion of standards and the institution of the media as a pillar of democracy. This includes closing the Broadcasting Standards Authority, the regulatory body governing radio and television – something experts have said is “politically expedient” and “democratically indefensible”.

None of these efforts have had any discernible effect on the way RNZ and TVNZ operate – and none of it is remotely comparable to the intimidation and interference happening in the US.

But if you had asked me three years ago if I could imagine Jeff Bezos prominently seated at Trump’s inauguration, then soon after aligning the Washington Post’s editorial page to Trumpian ideals, I would have laughed and said it wouldn’t – it couldn’t – happen. 

If there’s one thing I’ve learned over the past year, it’s not to take anything for granted.

The media sector in our small country is economically stressed: It’s battling international tech giants and AI models gobbling up digital revenue, and we’re all dealing with news fatigue and its cousin, hope fatigue.

The challenges are real, and becoming existential. Just look how many journalist jobs have been lost in the past decade (and it’s worsened in the past few years, with further job cuts and the closure of Newshub).

But there are still lots of journalists in New Zealand doing their very best in this tough environment, holding power to account on behalf of all of us. Because there’s another lesson for Aotearoa from the US: When the media is eroded or disappeared, our democracy clearly suffers. 

In the US, media analysts have noted the appearance of “news deserts” – places where there is virtually no credible local journalism. “Democracy suffers as citizens become less engaged and more polarised, and as government corruption flourishes because the watchdog has gone silent,” Margaret Sullivan, a former media columnist at the Washington Post and public editor at the New York Times, has written.

One study with a particularly jarring title, echoing the Post’s tagline – “Financing Dies in Darkness?” – found that when a newspaper closed, the city council had more trouble borrowing money. The markets concluded that local newspapers held their local governments accountable and kept costs low.

Other studies have shown that “news deserts” – in the US, as well as in the UK, Australia, Norway and Switzerland – have increased political polarisation, and reduced civic knowledge and voter turnout.

Despite everything that’s happened in the past few years, it is still clearly true that democracy does die in darkness. Here’s to sunlight.

Anna Fifield now writes about New Zealand’s place in the world on Substack and compiles the Spinoff’s weekly World Bulletin newsletter.
news.author: Anna Fifield

news.title: Obama to Tell 'the Brothers' to Vote for El-Sayed
news.text:
Former President Barack Obama will likely campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, the far-left Democrat who just won Michigan's U.S. Senate primary.

 The two spoke after the primary, and El-Sayed publicly said he hopes Obama will campaign for him. Michigan could determine control of the Senate, and Obama remains the most popular Democrat.

 El-Sayed won despite performing poorly among black primary voters. His coalition skewed younger, whiter, college-educated and progressive. In Detroit, Michigan's largest majority-black city, El-Sayed's opponent won more than 60% of the Democratic Senate vote. That may work in a Democratic primary. But will it work in November?

 Enter Obama.

 During the 2024 presidential campaign, Obama visited a Kamala Harris campaign office in Pittsburgh and said he wanted to "speak some truths." He complained that enthusiasm for Harris was weaker than when he ran and said the problem "seems to be more pronounced with the brothers."

 Obama said: "You're coming up with all kinds of reasons and excuses. I've got a problem with that," he said, suggesting some Black men "just aren't feeling the idea of having a woman as president."

 Apparently, some of "the brothers" remained unpersuaded. Pew Research Center's validated-voter analysis later estimated that 21% of black men voted for Donald Trump. Nevertheless, Obama will probably go to Michigan and explain to black voters who rejected El-Sayed in the primary why they should vote for him in November. After all, Obama and El-Sayed are closely aligned on policy.

 Take healthcare. El-Sayed supports Medicare for All. Obama repeatedly said the ideal healthcare plan would be single-payer. "If I were starting a system from scratch," Obama said in 2009, "then I think that the idea of moving towards a single-payer system could very well make sense." Near the end of his second term, Obama said, "If I was starting from scratch, I probably would have supported a single-payer system."

 Then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid called it a goal. Asked in 2013 whether Obamacare was ultimately a step toward single-payer healthcare, Reid answered, "Yes, yes. Absolutely, yes."

 Like Obama, El-Sayed chastises "the rich" for "not paying their fair share in taxes." Like Obama, who said racism is part of the America's "DNA," El-Sayed believes racism remains a serious problem.

 How far from Obama are these "far-left" Democrats? Last year, Obama called Democratic Socialist Zohran Mamdani during his campaign for New York City mayor, praised his campaign and reportedly offered to serve as a "sounding board."

 On Israel, there isn't much daylight between the two. El-Sayed has called the Israeli government "evil," "bloodthirsty" and a "rogue state." He declined to directly answer when asked, "Do you believe Israel has a right to exist?" Obama never went that far. He repeatedly defended Israel's legitimacy and security.

 But Obama and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu repeatedly clashed. Netanyahu fiercely opposed Obama's Iran nuclear deal, warning that Tehran could not be trusted. Israel obtained an archive of Iranian nuclear documents that Netanyahu said proved Iran was lying about its nuclear-weapons activities and was not abiding by the terms of the deal. The Obama-Netanyahu relationship became so poisonous that a senior Obama administration official reportedly called Netanyahu "chickens---." The White House distanced itself from the insult, but the hostility between the two leaders was no secret.

 What explains El-Sayed's weakness among black primary voters? In 2020, he explicitly said, "I believe we need to defund the police." Polls show blacks want the level of policing in their community to remain the same, if not increased. Blacks are disproportionately victims of crime. Tupac Shakur said: "The same crime element that white people are scared of black people are scared of ... Just because we black, we get along with the killers? What is that? We need protection, too."

 El-Sayed wants to abolish ICE, despite studies showing a connection between unskilled illegal aliens and lower wages and greater unemployment among black workers in the same skill group.

 This brings us back to Obama. El-Sayed needs black voters who did not particularly want him. Democrats need Michigan to gain control of the Senate.

 So, expect the former president to show up. And when he does, Obama will give "the brothers" a message. You may not have wanted this candidate. His positions may be against your self-interests.

 But vote for him anyway.

news.title: Is Mark Cuban FINALLY Figuring out His Side Is Nuts?
news.text:
In 2024, Mark Cuban tried hard to defend Kamala Harris' economic agenda, and it did not go well. The billionaire Shark Tank star tried, over and over, to sell voters on policies he clearly struggled to explain himself, and he got torched for it publicly and often. It was rough enough that Cuban announced he'd step back from politics after the election. He didn't. Within months, he was back to his usual anti-Trump routine on social media.

But a fight this week with Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) suggests Cuban may be starting to notice just how detached his own party has become. Will he finally see the light?

The blowup started over a proposed California wealth tax, tied to a ballot measure known as Prop 40, which Khanna and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) both support. The measure would slap a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of roughly 250 billionaires, and Cuban estimates it would raise about $20 billion a year for the state. Cuban's objection is simple: most startup founders are "cash poor, stock rich," meaning their net worth is tied to company shares rather than bank accounts. He questioned how a newly wealthy founder is supposed to pay a tax like that when no bank will lend against stock in a company that's barely a year old. Cuban isn't personally exposed since he doesn't live in California, but he said he'd require any startup he invests in to relocate to Dallas, Pittsburgh, or Indiana if the measure passes.

Ro, I like you. You know that. But you need to read the state of the state.The number of Deca Unicorns in Cali is growing by the day as investors chase amazing startups.A unique feature of these 10b startups is that even if they raise a billion, little, if any of that… https://t.co/l1LRaiki16— Mark Cuban (@mcuban) August 15, 2026

"Ideology is not a strategy, Ro," he wrote.

Khanna pushed back, arguing founders would only owe the tax if their companies actually succeeded, and wouldn't be personally liable if the business later failed. Nothing says “Welcome to California” like punishing success, right?

ICYMI: Sophie Cunningham Just Gave Leftists Another Reason to Hate Her

He invited Cuban to tour California, Pennsylvania, and other states to hear from ordinary voters, claiming most of them ask why the rate isn't higher than 5%. He also floated a fallback: if a founder couldn't pay, the state could simply sell his shares on his behalf.

That's when Cuban told Khanna flat-out, “You don’t understand business.”

And then he lost his cool.

"Ro, in your scenario, the founder could sell to pay a one-time 5% tax or the state could sell it if he defaults on the loan," Cuban wrote. "This is the biggest f**k you in the history of entrepreneurship. Ever. Creating jobs but don't have cash. F**k you. Can't sell shares, we will sell it for you, to whoever. F**k you. Creating jobs. Paying great wages instead of taking cash out yourself. F**k you. Reinvesting into your company and community. F**k you." He noted that executives like Jensen Huang and Lisa Su already sit on vast liquidity and don't object to taxes like this, and argued that's a world apart from someone who's poured years into a company only to be told a politician can liquidate it out from under him.

Ro, “in your scenario, the founder could sell to pay a one time 5 percent tax or the state could sell it if he defaults on the loan”Ro, this is the biggest fuck you in the history of entrepreneurship. Ever.Creating jobs but don’t have cash. Fuck youCan’t sell shares,… https://t.co/IYhoXVTSty— Mark Cuban (@mcuban) August 16, 2026

Khanna described his approach as “progressive capitalism,” comparing himself to FDR, who recruited General Motors executive Bill Knudsen to mobilize American industry.

If you’re reading between the lines, Khanna is probably running for president in 2028. But I digress.

Cuban countered that California already taxes income above $1 million at 13.3% and corporate earnings at 8.8%, and pointed out that 85% of the nation's venture capital went to California in the first quarter of 2026 alone, and that’s according to Khanna's own numbers. Cuban pointed out that voters would rather see lower everyday costs than one more one-time tax that funds almost nothing, all while driving higher-income business owners out of the state

Obviously, Cuban still isn't a conservative, and nobody should expect him to start voting like one. But watching a man who destroyed his own reputation to carry water for Kamala Harris erupt at a sitting Democrat for treating entrepreneurs like an ATM is worth noting. Maybe he's finally seeing what the rest of us already knew about his party. Maybe.

news.title: Katie Hobbs' running mate John Giles says GOP is a 'lost cause'
news.text:
John Giles left the Mesa mayor's office committed to remaining in the Republican Party, but joined Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs' ticket as an independent.

Giles said it simply became "a lost cause" to continue to advocate for the GOP, a party that drew him in with ideals of free enterprise and limited government but that he said has been forcing out more voters.

"I felt like I needed to be there to advocate for people like myself that were being shoved out of the party," he said. "A few months ago I realized that that’s a lost cause right now. Independent is a good place for me to be, it accurately describes where I’m at politically.”

Giles was a lifelong Republican who left the party in May, and is now not registered with any political party. He has supported Democrats, including Hobbs in 2022 and presidential hopeful Kamala Harris in 2024. He spoke at the Democratic National Convention that year.

Hobbs, who is seeking a second term in office this year, named Giles her running mate on Aug. 11. They have declined to be interviewed by The Arizona Republic, but took questions from reporters after a campaign event on Aug. 15 in Mesa.

The event was billed as an introduction of Giles and drew a friendly group of about 100 people to his law office, Udall Shumway. Giles said those supporters had a choice: Republican gubernatorial hopeful Andy Biggs, who Giles dismissed as "Washington Andy" for prioritizing partisan politics, or "Arizona Katie," who would tackle the state's nonpartisan issues.

Giles acknowledged that other than past partisan affiliation, he has a lot in common with Hobbs, who has campaigned on issues that often align with conservative ideals like tax cuts and growing business.

Asked to identify something they don’t agree on, Giles said there was "remarkably little or nothing."

They might differ on approach, he said. "But we share a common agenda for what our priorities are going to be and those are nonpartisan agenda items," Giles said, naming transportation and education.

On some of the state's most high-profile issues, the pair is aligned. Hobbs and Giles agree there should be guardrails on the state's school voucher program and supported a ballot measure enshrining abortion rights in 2024, for example.

Hobbs said Giles' role in her second term, if she is elected again in November, had not yet been determined. By law, he must serve as her chief of staff, head of a state agency or another role that the governor gets to appoint.

"As mayor he brings so much expertise in the work he did in Mesa to grow the economy, to expand educational opportunity, and so I’m really excited to have that in my administration and we’ll figure out where that fits best," Hobbs said.

First elected by a sliver four years ago, Hobbs is asking Arizonans to give her a second term in what is likely to be one of the toughest gubernatorial races in the nation. For the first time in state history, the campaign includes choosing a running mate to serve as lieutenant governor. Arizona voters created the position in 2022, and that person would fill the shoes of the governor if the governor cannot complete their term.

Biggs, a longtime congressman and former state lawmaker, previously chose Sine Kerr to be his No. 2 if he is elected. Kerr was a dairy farmer for decades and represented a conservative district stretching from the West Valley to Yuma in the state Senate.

news.title: Biden, Walsh wade into Massachusetts's Sixth District primary
news.text:
The exchange encapsulated Koh’s approach, and the kind of help he’s getting, in the six-way primary. As Democrats here and elsewhere try to pitch voters on the need for wholesale change, Koh is leaning on his years spent inside government offices — and on his famous former bosses — to help deliver the message.

Koh and Walsh spent Wednesday shaking hands and giving hugs among the crowd attending a concert-in-the-park series. The same week, Walsh, who also campaigned for Koh during his unsuccessful 2018 bid in the Third Congressional District, visited seniors and attended a canvass with Koh. Then on Thursday, Koh, the former White House aide, released a new television ad featuring smiling cameos from former President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris.

Walsh said he plans to be out “as much as I can be” in the days before the Sept. 1 primary, calling himself “a friend helping a friend.” Still, he and Biden are the type of surrogates few can trot out — and perhaps that others aren’t clamoring to campaign alongside.

The race to replace Representative Seth Moulton in the North Shore-anchored district has mirrored a debate coursing through the Democratic Party: Do voters want to cut ties with the party’s old guard amid calls for a new generation of leaders? Or is the party — and Washington, D.C. — best fixed by those who bear some political battle scars?

The other Democrats in the race are veering hard into the former. For instance, John Beccia, a Lynnfield fintech executive who has put $3 million of his own money into his bid, cast both Koh and Nguyen as “corrupt politicians,” pointing to a report that Koh’s stock portfolio grew while he served in the White House. (Koh’s campaign said he did not buy or sell individual stocks during his time there, and Koh has advocated for banning stock trading by members of Congress.)

Beccia, like Koh, has framed himself as the best option to counter President Trump, saying in an ad released Wednesday that he’d “stand up to Trump’s corruption and work with anyone to get things done for working families.”

Nguyen, for her part, has called on her opponents to release the last five years of their tax returns, looking to draw attention to their relative wealth compared to her modest upbringing as a refugee from Vietnam who grew up in public housing. That, she’s argued, gives her an “outsider” perspective as she’s also leaned on her Beacon Hill experience and dozens of endorsements from sitting lawmakers.

“My opponents shouldn’t have any trouble meeting this minimum transparency standard,” Nguyen said in a statement about her tax return push, “particularly those who are eagerly using their insider connections and personal wealth to fund their campaigns.”

The race also includes former state representative Jamie Belsito; Mariah Lancaster, a former federal worker and veterinarian of Salem; and Middleton software engineer Bethany Andres-Beck.

That criticism — and his opponents’ increased attacks on his D.C. connections — hasn’t deterred Koh from emphasizing his lengthy political resume. And it’s one Walsh, who has advocated on Koh’s behalf by leaning on local labor leaders, argues he shouldn’t be criticized for.

“I have personally given money to candidates all across the United States of America,” Walsh told the Globe. “They should not be criticized because I gave them a donation from Boston or Massachusetts.”

Koh has simultaneously emphasized his Biden ties, praising the former president as many Democrats have grown cool toward him since 2024. His latest ad featured very brief cameos from Biden and Harris — and more than a dozen photos from his White House days — meant to underscore his pitch that he’s “the only candidate with the experience to take on Trump.” It’s a rare appearance from both Biden and Harris on behalf of a candidate this cycle.

Then there’s the in-person appearances. Though Walsh, the executive director of the NHL Players’ Association, is technically no longer in politics and doesn’t vote in the Sixth District, his name and image still appeared to carry some weight. At the Andover concert Wednesday evening, he moved from lawn chair to lawn chair with ease, taking photos and shaking hands with attendees as he talked up Koh.

One parent turned to her son as Walsh passed, pointing and whispering, “That’s the guy that worked with Biden.”

Walsh said he’s told Koh since his unsuccessful 2018 bid for Congress, “You gain more in a loss sometimes than you do in victory” — in this case, his Washington experience. Koh has also worked under Walsh since both left the Biden administration: He disclosed making $180,000 last year as a “technology” consultant for the NHL Players’ Association.

Still, while many Andover concertgoers told the pair they had Koh lawn signs or were familiar with his family, a good number said they were undecided — or had yet to tune into the race at all.

“I like that they’re not completely attacking each other,” Eric Farmer, a 60-year-old Andover resident, said of the Democrats running, adding that he otherwise hadn’t decided who to support.

Wentzel, the North Andover resident who spoke with Walsh, said he likes Koh but still came away undecided, praising both Koh and Nguyen, whom he feels “has been a very good rep for the people of her district.”

“On my front lawn, you might see a sign for Dan, and you might see a sign for Tram,” Wentzel said, noting that his wife is backing Nguyen. “Whoever wins, it’s going to be good for the district.”

news.title: A Democratic Civil War Is Brewing in Trump's Home State
news.text: Ahead of the November midterms, Democrats will settle a fight this week in Florida, a state that President Donald Trump now calls home, that the rest of the party has been having all summer. Three insurgent candidates are on the ballot in Florida’s August 18 primary, each challenging a better-funded establishment Democrat. All three are making a similar argument: that “electability” has become a way for the Democratic Party to decide which candidates are viable before voters get a chance to choose. Oliver Larkin is challenging U.S. Representative Jared Moskowitz in the 25th Congressional District. Elijah Manley is one of several candidates running against U.S. Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz in the redrawn 20th District. Florida state Representative Angie Nixon is running for the Democratic nomination in the special U.S. Senate election against retired U.S. Army Lieutenant Colonel Alexander Vindman. Michigan Representative Rashida Tlaib, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), was scheduled to appear at a Fort Lauderdale rally Friday to support all three candidates, according to organizers. The event, called “Chomp the Oligarchy,” was hosted by Miami DSA, Broward County DSA, Gen Z for Change and the Florida Youth Justice Coalition. The original venue canceled after local Democrats objected, so organizers moved the event. Florida Republican Representative Randy Fine criticized the congresswoman's visit, telling Fox News Digital it was "no coincidence" Tlaib, the only Palestinian American currently serving in Congress, was campaigning against two of the chamber's remaining Jewish Democrats. The three candidates do not all describe themselves the same way. Larkin openly identifies as a democratic socialist while Manley calls himself a progressive and economic populist. His endorsements this cycle have come from California Representative Ro Khanna, a Democrat, the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, Florida Rising and Dream Defenders, rather than the national DSA. Conservative outlets covering Tlaib’s visit including Fox News and The Washington Examiner have described both men as socialists. In a previous statement to Newsweek, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said that “the Democrats’ full-blown embrace of socialism and communism is a mortal threat to American liberty," adding that "President Trump will never allow America to become a socialist or communist country.” Newsweek has contacted Nixon, Wasserman Schultz, and Moskowitz for comment via email. The Electability Fight In separate interviews with Newsweek, Larkin and Manley made nearly identical cases against the standard the party applies to candidates like them. "The electability argument, the how electable a candidate is being directly tied in with how many corporate PAC donations or how moderate they are on issues, I think that's just gone completely out the window after the 2024 election, losing a second nationwide election to Donald Trump," Larkin said. He pointed to the top of that ticket. "Kamala Harris lost every single swing state in the country in 2024." Manley said Democrats have turned “electability” and “viability” into standards that are used to shut out progressive candidates. "Electability has been kind of weaponized in a way to progressives against Democrats in general," he said. "And it's not just the word electability; it's the word viability too. The only way you can determine whether or not somebody is electable is when an election is held." Manley argued the standard is applied unevenly. "People tend to use the word electability and viability against candidates of color the most," he said. "And against women, against candidates of color, Black candidates specifically." He named Nixon directly. "People say that Angie Nixon is unelectable. I disagree." Both candidates rejected the idea that the party's path runs through moderate voters. "There's this myth of the middle, this myth that there's a voter in the middle that can be wooed over," Manley said. He argued Democratic voters stay home rather than defect. "Why would I vote for a Republican light when I could just have the Republican? If I'm going to go for a Coke and someone says, do you want a Diet Coke? I'm going to say no." Larkin framed the same point as arithmetic. "Electoralism is a game of addition, not subtraction," he said. What the Polls and the Markets Say The numbers do not favor them. Prediction markets give Moskowitz roughly 88 to 90 percent odds of winning the nomination, with Larkin in the low double digits. In District 20, markets price Wasserman Schultz around 91 percent. On Polymarket, Vindman has traded near 94 percent in the Senate primary, with Nixon at 6 percent. Polling has been less settled. An EMC Research survey commissioned by the Wasserman Schultz campaign in early May found her taking 52 percent of likely primary voters in a field of eight. A separate Listener Group poll conducted from May 29 to June 1 found her at 39 percent on an initial ballot with Manley at 21 percent, then showed Manley moving from an 18-point deficit to a 9-point lead once voters heard biographical information about the candidates. That poll also found Manley beating Wasserman Schultz 63 percent to 37 percent in a head-to-head matchup. Manley cited that gap as evidence against reading early surveys as verdicts. "Polls are a snapshot into a moment," he said. "They don't tell the full story." Larkin, meanwhile, said his own race has tightened. "We're still the underdog, but we are closing at a very rapid pace," he said, citing roughly 40,000 doors knocked and more than a quarter million voter contact attempts. He said he has been outspent by $650,000 from two super PACs. Nixon offers the clearest data point on the electability question, and it cuts both ways. A University of North Florida Public Opinion Research Lab survey of 848 likely midterm voters, released in July, found Republican Senator Ashley Moody leading Nixon 50 percent to 42 percent. Moody led Vindman by an even wider margin, 50 percent to 40 percent. Nixon ran two points closer despite a massive fundraising disadvantage. A competing Change Research poll, conducted July 9–11 for Freedom Project USA, a group aligned with Vindman, showed a very different race. It found Vindman leading Nixon 39 percent to 24 percent, with 36 percent of voters undecided. The fundraising gap is stark. Vindman has reported raising $16.7 million, while Nixon has raised just over $625,000 and had about $118,000 cash on hand at the end of June. Nixon has said she is not worried about appealing to Florida's independent and no-party-affiliation voters. She is endorsed by Representative Rashida Tlaib, Representative Ilhan Omar, the Service Employees International Union and the Working Families Party. In May, the Florida House Rules and Ethics Committee reprimanded her after she used a megaphone during a protest that disrupted a vote on the state's new congressional maps. “We are not going to leave any stone unturned at all,” Nixon told Jacksonville Today. “This campaign is not about politics as usual. It's about returning the power back into the hands of the people.” Vindman's campaign said it has attracted 235,000 unique donors, with an average contribution of less than $40. It said 98 percent of donations were under $200 and that Vindman does not accept corporate PAC money. “The choice is clear: if you want an outsider who is ready to disrupt the status quo, I'm your guy,” Vindman said in a statement to Newsweek. He pointed to his “Florida First Agenda,” which includes lowering homeowners' insurance, gas and housing costs, and banning congressional stock trading. The National Wave The Florida races arrive at the end of what some on the left have called "hot DSA summer." DSA-endorsed candidates have unseated three sitting House Democrats this cycle in New York, Colorado and Michigan. Melat Kiros defeated Colorado Representative Diana DeGette, a moderate Democrat first elected in 1997, while Donavan McKinney defeated Michigan Representative Shri Thanedar. In New York, insurgents Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier also won their primaries, while Chris Rabb won an open seat in the Philadelphia area. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive who does not identify as a democratic socialist, defeated Michigan Representative Haley Stevens for the Democratic Senate nomination. The streak broke last week in Wisconsin, where democratic socialist Francesca Hong narrowly lost the gubernatorial primary to David Crowley. The Democratic establishment saw it as a limitation, but Manley saw it differently. "She barely lost," he said. "She lost by like 2,000, 3,000 votes out of hundreds of thousands cast. That's not a movement they can just throw to the side." Hong has become the party establishment's reference point in the days since, cited as evidence that democratic socialists cannot close the deal outside safe urban seats. CNN reported the result was met with relief by top Democrats who had feared she would drag down the ticket in a state the party needs in November. Manley said the comparison does not hold. "I think it's the wrong pitch. It's the wrong assumption, because the neighboring state just picked Abdul El-Sayed to be the nominee," he said. "They can't just point to one race." He also said the label attached to Hong is the same one he is fighting. "We just saw this in Wisconsin with Francesca Hong," he said. "Maybe that's a situation where it may or may not have been true, but people tend to use the word electability and viability against candidates of color the most. Voters are not hive minds." The Socialism Problem in South Florida Florida is a tougher test than New York or Denver, in part because of the state's political history and the views of its large Latino electorate. The state is home to roughly 1.9 million Cuban Americans, at least 900,000 of them in Miami-Dade County, along with large Venezuelan and Nicaraguan populations. A 2021 Equis Research report found that four in 10 Latino voters in 2020 were concerned that Democrats were embracing socialism, including 30 percent of those who voted for Joe Biden. NBC News/Telemundo polling has also found that a plurality of Latino voters view socialism negatively, though views vary by age and ideology. Nationally, Gallup found that positive views of capitalism fell to 54 percent last August, the lowest level since 2010. Views of socialism have changed little over the past 15 years, with 39 percent viewing it positively and 57 percent negatively. Larkin argued that the national party has misread Florida entirely. "Florida is one of the most elastic states in the country," he said. "The national media and the Democratic Party has been very quick to drop Florida like a hot potato, like it's just written off." Manley pointed to the party's closest recent statewide race as evidence. "The closest we ever got to winning statewide was with Andrew Gillum, a Black progressive candidate," he said. "He came 30,000 votes within beating Ron DeSantis. Since then, since we haven't had the progressive statewide candidate, we have lost by huge margins." What Democrats Fear About November Republicans have been explicit about wanting the matchup. "Democrats want voters to believe the DSA is a Los Angeles or a Brooklyn problem, confined to urban enclaves, harmless beyond big cities," Republican strategist Matt Klink told Newsweek. "The problem is that DSA-aligned candidates are now winning primaries in non-urban districts, which hands Republicans a ready-made argument that extends well beyond the coasts and straight into November." Jim Kessler of the centrist Democratic group Third Way argued that progressive Democrats have yet to prove they can win outside heavily Democratic districts, and that their support can erode when their positions on issues like crime come under scrutiny. "They have not yet shown the ability to win general elections except in very blue places. And for the most part, when they managed to win their popularity has fallen as their radical views on issues like crime come back to haunt them," Kessler told Newsweek. When asked what he would tell conservative voters who see positions like his call to abolish the Senate as extreme, Larkin pointed to the cost of living. "I'm running to address people's concerns right now, lowering the cost of living, expanding Social Security, making the billionaires and ultra wealthy pay their fair share into the taxation system," he said. "I'm not trying to take anything away from people. I'm trying to improve their material conditions." The party also has an unresolved dispute over race. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has declined to endorse Wasserman Schultz, a plurality-Black district, after Black officials objected to her decision to run there. "This seat is going to be a catalyst," Manley said. "If she wins, it's going to be the catalyst for other people across the country in our party to take away Black representation." Larkin said he would back the winner regardless. "I'll support the Democratic nominee," he said. "Electing a Republican in this seat is unacceptable," adding that Moskowitz has not made the same commitment publicly. Early voting ends Sunday. Polls close Tuesday. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Jason Lemon and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: Three insurgent candidates are on the ballot in Florida’s August 18 primary, each challenging a better-funded moderate Democrat.

news.title: Trump's terrifying secret prisons that epitomise his America
news.text:
To celebrate 50 years of independence from Britain, the kingdom of Swaziland changed its name to Eswatini in 2018. I had to look up the tiny nation on a map to find it was landlocked between South Africa and Mozambique. This houses America’s newest version of Guantanamo Bay – but it’s a detention camp for deportees, not terrorists.

The New York Times Magazine has just published a chilling article about the fate of an inmate: “He was Deported to a Country He’d Never Heard Of. He May Never Go Free.” This tells the terrifying, Kafkaesque story of Roberto Mosquera, a Cuban who was forced onto a military cargo plane in Texas and deposited in a maximum security prison in Eswatini last year.

Mosquera arrived in the US aged 12 from Cuba. As a teenager, he joined a gang and served time for attempted murder after shooting a rival gangster in the leg. At this point, I can feel your sympathy waver. But on his release, he settled down, became a plumber, married, had four daughters – and led a normal life as long as he checked in with US immigration authorities every year. He is now 59.

In June 2025, Mosquera went to renew his visa, as usual, and was transported to Eswatini. Cuba will not take back US detainees and he has no idea how long he will be stuck in a harsh, friendless prison on the other side of the world. The US is paying undisclosed millions to Eswatini and other countries to keep immigrants like him in limbo. It’s a horror story.

“Do you think I’ll ever get out of here?” Mosquera asked the New York Times reporter, who managed to speak to him by phone. Nobody knows. The US department of homeland security celebrated his deportation (with four other detainees) last year with a cruel social media post about “depraved monsters” who were “so uniquely barbaric their home countries refused to take them back”.

This isn’t who Mosquera is. But is this what America has become? A place of secret flights, disappearances and rendition? This is the terrifying reality behind Donald Trump’s mass deportation policy. While the President slumbers in his golden Oval Office and finds new ways to drape himself in praise, people are being thrown into oubliettes where they are left to rot.

The cruelty is the point. Does anybody care? The world took notice when Renee Good and Alex Pretti were killed by immigration agents at anti-ICE protests in Minneapolis last winter. “Operation Metro Surge” was halted. But the arrests, deportations and disappearances have continued. 

These frequently occur when immigrants are just checking in, like Mosquera, and behaving responsibly. Often, they simply go missing until families, friends or employers start alerting the police and find they have been detained. 

In July last year, an administration order blandly called “Interim Guidance Regarding Detention Authority” gave Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents the authority to detain people “regardless of length of residency and community ties to the US” and stipulated “continuous custody” until they are removed. 

Although the courts are getting choked up with appeals, most people are helpless to defend themselves. The Department of Homeland Security insists, “The law is on our side”. It told Politico this week: “ICE is not slowing down.” There are currently 65,000 ICE detainees held in 200 jails or temporary, makeshift sites in America. They are full to bursting. In June, 300,000 Haitians lost Temporary Protected Status allowing them to work in the US, so ICE has begun ordering them to check-in with the authorities to be issued with ankle monitors instead.

Remember the Haitians in Springfield, Ohio? Fired up by his running mate JD Vance, Trump wildly and falsely claimed during a presidential debate with Kamala Harris: “In Springfield they are eating the dogs… they are eating the cats.”

Springfield’s 16,000 Haitians have been the first in their state to receive letters ordering them to check in, according to local news reports this week. “When they do, their passports are collected,” said Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church. “They’re fitted with ankle [monitors]; I call them ankle shackles.”

They are not criminals and have done nothing wrong. In fact, the Republican governor of Ohio, Mike DeWine, said they had revitalised Springfield’s economy by taking on manufacturing and other blue-collar jobs. Now they’re being placed in shackles, like slaves, in a northern, midwest state that fought for the Union during the Civil War. 

The American people had their say at the last election. But the result under Trump is a sprawling, secretive shadowland of suffering that is rarely heard about and mostly ignored. 

Sarah Baxter is Director of the Marie Colvin Center for International Reporting

news.title: SC to hold first 2028 Democratic primary. What it means for candidates
news.text:
Since 1992, anytime a Democrat has won the White House, South Carolina primary voters have picked the winning candidate. Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden were the top vote-getters in the state on their roads to the presidency.

As Democrats seek a path back to 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. in 2028, South Carolina will again be the first state in the nation to hold a Democratic presidential primary – or at least the state sanctioned by party leaders to vote first. The Democratic National Committee officially confirmed Aug. 15 that South Carolina is the party's choice to replace Iowa and New Hampshire, the traditional leadoff states, in two years to better reflect the party’s diverse voters.

More: Democrats approve 2028 early voting plan, demoting NH and IA

Many potential presidential candidates are already making pilgrimages to the state, even though the primary won't happen until Jan. 22, 2028.

That includes multiple trips by California Gov. Gavin Newsom for the South Carolina Democratic Party's "On the Road" series, an initiative designed to connect national and regional Democratic figures to local communities.

Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly participated in a SCDP town hall event in 2025. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear was an SCDP speaker earlier in 2026. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, Democrats' unsuccessful 2024 candidate, participated in a private fundraiser this year. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, the latter a 2020 presidential candidate, took part in this year's "On the Road" series.

“Everybody comes here to test the water,” said Brent Nelsen, a political science professor at Furman University in Greenville, South Carolina. “Because we have a significant African American population, it is a great place for Democratic candidates to test their message with one of the main foundational blocks of the Democratic coalition.”

More than 60% of South Carolina’s Democratic primary electorate is African American, which is the party's most reliable voting bloc. Matters of faith and affordability are the most important issues for voters, and a moderate candidate is likely to do best here, say the state's Democratic leaders and political experts.

South Carolina is in the Bible belt

South Carolina voters tend to be conservative and deeply religious, and candidates who can speak to their religious or spiritual beliefs would do well, said Christale Spain, chair of the South Carolina Democratic Party.

“It is a part of how you have to campaign in the Deep South,” said Spain. “It’s the Bible belt.”

Spain said while faith communities are part of the political landscape, dominated mostly by Baptists and Methodists, it doesn’t mean that people from other denominations or religions would be at a disadvantage.

“I mean, Joe Biden was a Catholic,” she said.

Political commentator Bakari Sellers, a former member of the South Carolina House of Representatives, agreed.

"Rooted in faith is important. It's not a religiosity, although, you know, Black Christianity is extremely strong, but it's having some center of faith," he said. "At the end of the day, we want somebody who understands the power of prayer."

He pointed to Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who is Jewish, and Moore, who is a Southern Baptist.

"Both come in with the ability to understand the power of faith, the power of prayer, and they can do well," he said.

Candidates willing to 'do the work' and increase voter turnout

Rep. Jim Clyburn, South Carolina’s only Democratic congressman, is seen as a kingmaker in the state party, and in an Aug. 3 interview with Roland Martin, he said Black voters should not be taken for granted.

“The fact of the matter is you want to win in November. So you ought to put people on the field who demonstrate that they can appeal to all those corners that make up this party," said Clyburn, an influential member of the Congressional Black Caucus. "The African American vote is very important to the Democratic Party."

Successful candidates will be able to inspire turnout, Clyburn said, noting that only about 59% of eligible Black voters cast ballots in 2024.

South Carolina Democrats will gravitate to candidates who are willing to do the work of connecting with voters and helping Democratic candidates win in the state, Spain said.

“The candidate that wants to help South Carolina Democrats break the Republican supermajority of the State House. The candidate that wants to help Dr. Anna Andrews become the next junior senator from South Carolina. The candidate that wants to help elect the next Democratic governor in South Carolina,” Spain said. “That's who does well in South Carolina.”

The state's voters also want candidates who can connect with them on issues of affordability.

"Someone who can speak to the pain that everybody feels across the country," said Spain. "The cost of gas, the cost of groceries, access to affordable health care, education – all those things matter to South Carolinians just like they matter to Democratic voters across the country."

Among candidates with buzz, she said, are Newsom and Booker.

“I don't know that there's one name that rises above the others, but you have people like Governor Newsom, because he made national headlines for all the work he's done to push back against the unconstitutional redistricting,” she said.

Booker has “great relationships” from the time he ran for president in 2020 and had a big team on the ground, she said.

Progressives vs. moderates

While the Democratic Party is facing an ongoing ideological tug-of-war between the moderate establishment and its progressive wing nationwide, moderates still have an edge in the conservative state, say the state's party leadership and political experts.

The decision to put South Carolina first is one of the smartest strategic moves the DNC has made in a long time, said Melissa DeRosa, a national Democratic strategist.

“It will reward the candidate who can assemble the core Democratic coalition – not simply excite the loudest, most homogeneous fringe faction of the party," she said.

Did she have a guess on who might do well?

“We’ll see on the ‘who,’ but it unquestionably favors candidates who start early, have money and organization, build real relationships in South Carolina, can win over Jim Clyburn,” DeRosa said. “And understand that social media buzz is no substitute for working-class support.”

Sellers doesn't think far-left progressive candidates such as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York will do well among the traditional Democratic base voters in the state.

“South Carolina is going to cull the herd extremely early,” he said. “This isn’t where a far-left movement is going to come through and sweep the state … where someone like AOC will be able to bring far left-ideologies into the environment and be persuasive or victorious.”

Ocasio-Cortez hasn't said whether she will run in 2028. Another progressive thought to be considering running is Rep. Ro Khanna of California. He served as the SCDP state convention keynote speaker this year.

Gibbs Knotts, professor of political science at Coastal Carolina University and author of the 2020 book "First in the South: Why South Carolina’s Presidential Primary Matters,” said the state has often played the role of tiebreaker when Iowa and New Hampshire, traditionally the first two states to hold primaries, picked different candidates.

This time, it is slated to play a different role than it's had before, he said, and the person who emerges on top in South Carolina is likely to be a moderate Democrat, as the state's voters tend to be a "little more conservative on the ideological spectrum."

"Most progressive candidates, I think, will struggle some in South Carolina, given the Democratic electorate and the political culture in the state,” he said.

Sellers cast the progressive movement in the country as a "suburban, white, upper crust type of movement."

"That doesn't mesh with what we have here in South Carolina," he said.

Sellers' top picks for who might do well? Moore, Beshear and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, in no particular order. They are all viewed as mainstream, pragmatic Democrats, he said.

He classified Newsom as a "somewhat unknown quantity."

“He has name ID coming into the state, but again, the ‘I am the smartest person and the most handsome person in the room, all you have to do is ask me' type of candidacy doesn't necessarily play well here,” said Sellers. “So, we'll see how that works for him as well.”

'Hunger for something different'

While the state is traditional and not prone to radicalism, Nelsen said there’s an appetite for change.

“I hear it on the streets that there's this hunger for something different, something exciting, something that you can really get excited about,” he said. “So perhaps an AOC or somebody else emerges.”

Still, he said he’d be surprised if a Democratic Socialists of America candidate won in South Carolina, adding that he doesn’t see Clyburn backing such a candidate.

“But I would not be surprised that a DSA candidate had a very strong showing that might then propel that person to stronger showings in subsequent primaries,” he said.

Once the November midterm elections are over, it is going to be interesting to see how the two big factions in the Democratic Party play in South Carolina, Nelsen said.

Spain was optimistic about progressives' chances.

"I think they'll play well in South Carolina," said Spain, who worked on Sen. Bernie Sanders' 2016 presidential campaign.

However, she said, progressive candidates who have gone to Iowa and New Hampshire for decades would have to make the same level of investment in South Carolina and be "unafraid to speak to issues that matter to the Black community and help uplift those issues as well."

Candidates' efforts to focus on South Carolina could be complicated by threats from Iowa and New Hampshire Democrats to hold their 2028 nominating contests first, regardless of the national party's decision on a calendar.

Kamala Harris is not a given

Early presidential polls suggest Harris has a head start on the Democratic field, but it's not a given that she'll do well in South Carolina, Knotts said.

“I mean, she is from California. And so the ability to sort of connect with Southern voters would be something that you'd want to look at,” Knotts said.

The Democratic National Committee's autopsy of why the party lost the 2024 election, released this year, cited Harris' inability to energize voters as one of the reasons.

"Losing a whopping 6.8 million voters who supported Biden in 2020 proved pivotal in this extremely close election," the autopsy report said. "Harris's inability to mobilize these pro-Biden voters may have been the campaign's biggest failure."

While Sellers and Spain said Harris has a good chance in the 2028 primary, Nelsen wasn’t optimistic.

“I think there's very little enthusiasm for her. I’m on a college campus, and no one has emerged as a clear favorite for anybody," said Nelsen. "People kind of screw up their faces when Newsom is mentioned. I think it’s a wide-open field.”

His top three picks? Shapiro, Moore and Newsom.

Knotts also cited Moore as having the potential to do well.

With 524 days until the South Carolina Democratic primary, "potential" is the operative word.

news.title: 'I got the s**t kicked out of me - but it made me realise who I needed to help'
news.text: Walking into Westminster's Strangers' Bar on his third day in Parliament, brand-new political staffer Pablo O'Hana came up against the stuffy elitism of British politics. Aged 19 and a brand-new staffer for Manchester Liberal Democrat MP John Leech, he was introduced to another MP in the bar who shook his hand and asked: "Which one did you go to?" The question took Pablo aback; not only did it come barely seconds after their introduction, but its meaning wasn't immediately obvious. He soon realised the MP was referring to which university he attended: "Oxford or Cambridge?" The surreal moment made him realise just how at odds his own upbringing in Withington was compared to the MPs and staffers he would now rub shoulders with at the bar. Especially when taking into account that he had never attended university, not helped by his 'hellish' school years in Manchester, which left him with few qualifications. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter "I was actually all right in primary school," Pablo said. "Secondary school was where everything went off the rails. "I mean, it's easy now to look back and think, 'Well, you know, I did ballet, I had a passion for animal rights, I was obsessed with Titanic.' Now I look back and think, well, no wonder I had the s**t kicked out of me!" Pablo, now 32, recalls in his first week at secondary school being approached at a bus stop by a group of boys from the same school who beat him so badly he ended up in hospital. He says the reason for the attack, something his assailants made clear, was his sexuality. It was something the boys immediately picked up on, making him a target. It would not be an isolated incident. The five years of secondary school often saw him singled out for threats and violence, including being kicked down a set of stairs. However, he later became less isolated when he befriended a group of girls and found a member of staff who was sympathetic to his interest in the arts. It was with this teacher that Pablo discovered he could pursue his interests in technical theatre and poster design. However, the bullying and what Pablo describes as being "written off" by others at the school meant he left school with barely any GCSEs. In his spare time, Pablo also ran a fan site for pop star-turned-actress Billie Piper. Pablo says she later invited him to London, where they arranged to work on her social media presence as she transitioned from music to acting. It was a job that "opened a million doors", he said. Around the same time, he moved to Belfast after getting a job in public relations at the Titanic exhibition. Yet despite falling in love with the city, Manchester soon came calling him back. A social media position was advertised in his home city to help get Liberal Democrat MP John Leech re-elected to the Council in 2016. The campaign was ultimately successful, and John Leech has been MP for West Didsbury ever since. It was as part of Mr Leech's team that Pablo found himself introduced to another MP in a Westminster bar and asked whether he went to Oxford or Cambridge. Strange circumstances indeed for someone who confesses to having flunked both his GCSEs and A-Levels and subsequently never went to university at all. Pablo continued to help rebuild the Liberal Democrat party after its coalition with the Conservatives ended in 2015. It was during this time, Pablo says experienced something of an epiphany, witnessing the sincere passion of the party's new leader, Tim Farron, to resolve the Syrian refugee crisis. "That was when I began to see the difference that a national politician could make," said Pablo. This realisation spurred him to continue working behind the scenes as an advisor for the Liberal Democrats on local, national, and European elections. Pablo also found himself increasingly passionate about women's rights, and later worked on the successful campaign to legalise abortion in Ireland in 2018. "Anyone who works in politics will tell you even if they're just behind the scenes like me... they have a thing that really motivates them," Pablo said. "So the first MP I ever worked for was really motivated by things like social housing, LGBT rights... that kind of thing. For me, it was always women's rights, and I could never really figure it out until I talked it through with a therapist. "He was like, 'It's actually not at all surprising that the people who protected you in school were the girls.' And as you've gone into a position of power, like you are now. "The theme throughout your political campaigns has all been about pushing forward abortion rights, working for the first female leader of the Liberal Democrats, working for Kamala Harris." Not content with European politics, Pablo's desire to work with people who shared his passions led him to plunge headfirst into US politics. First, as a volunteer, he helped elect Letitia James, the first black woman elected stateside in New York. Before being recruited as an advisor to help Joe Biden, and later Kamala Harris' bid to beat Donald Trump to the White House in 2024. Ultimately, despite his considerable track record in helping politicians get their message across, his campaign to help Kamala Harris become the first woman US President was unsuccessful. Before the election, Pablo says there was a moment while he was over in the US when he knew support for Donald Trump was growing and that Kamala Harris' campaign was in trouble. "I remember driving down the motorway, and I was fairly convinced that we were in trouble. I was pretty sure that we were not going to win," Pablo said. "I did an awful lot of media, I was on GB News and TalkTV and Sky, like defending, defending, defending, but secretly knowing that it was going to be tough. "And this car pulled up alongside me, and they were honking. I turned ready to flip a finger, assuming that they were having a go at me for not going fast enough or something. "And I saw this black mother driving, and next to her was this little girl, this black girl, and she had got a cardboard box, and she had ripped the side of it, and she'd written in three colours 'Kamala'. "My heart shattered, because I was fairly sure we were going to lose. It's those moments that carry the weight for me, because I am always conscious of why I do what I do. “But it's in those moments I thought, 'Oh my god, that mum tomorrow is going to have to wake up and tell her daughter just to wait a few more years.' "And it honestly it killed me. I turned and I waved, and kind of stretched this fake smile on my face. The whole way to [Washington] DC, I just had this empty feeling in my stomach, it was just awful." Pablo has since returned to the UK as head of his own public relations agency, Apostrophe Campaigns, in Manchester city centre. He has returned to the UK feeling a lot more optimistic, even patriotic, about the UK since his experiences in America. And despite his affiliations to the Liberal Democrats, he says he feels a greater sense of hope in the country since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister. But mostly, he wants to see the former Greater Manchester Mayor overhaul the UK's education system. A system he still feels failed him, despite finding a different path to success. "We need to embrace what kids are passionate about," Pablo said. "In a sense, I'm lucky that I was completely unembarrassed in my passions. I loved Billie Piper, I loved Titanic, I cared about animal rights, and I was not going to let any of those go, no matter how bad things got." Also contemplating dipping his toe back into US politics, Pablo feels that, despite not having a university education, his future is bright. He’s not the only one. Didsbury West MP John Leech agrees, telling the M.E.N. that Pablo was an integral part of the small team that got him re-elected to the Council in 2016. Adding Pablo was in charge of his social media: "At a time where politicians are often seen as out of touch with reality, he managed to make me seem fairly human. “I am not at all surprised that he has gone on to bigger and better things, because he is the best at what he does."
news.summary: Advisor to some of the UK and US' top politicians, 32-yera-old Pablo O'Hana from Withington left school with few qualifications and never went to university

news.title: Former Bernie Sanders operative warns radical left has ‘overtaken’ the Democratic Party from within
news.text:
A former Bernie Sanders operative is sounding the alarm over what the Democratic Party has become, warning the far left has “overtaken” the party from within.

“Part of the reason it’s been overtaken is because the establishment tried really hard in 2020 to block us, and in 2019, after AOC won, they did a blacklist, and that actually backfired on them. And it made the far left grow stronger,” Evan Barker told “Jesse Watters Primetime.”

Barker, who raised money for Democratic candidates throughout her career before deciding to vote for Trump in 2024, argued that the Democratic establishment’s efforts to contain its insurgent flank ultimately backfired, pushing activists to build their own political infrastructure, from training one another to recruiting donors, including billionaires.

The result, Barker argued, is a party increasingly influenced from the inside by its activist base, donors and staffers, some of whom she says are considerably further left than the politicians they work for.

“I think they’ve kind of been captured from all sides. They have these hyper-left-leaning donors coupled with the staff that’s been radicalized and the base,” she said.

Barker said she has watched that shift play out even within the movement she once joined, pointing to Sanders’ positions on issues, including guns and immigration.

“I’ve seen him kind of be dragged further and further to the left by what he views as his message bearers, people like AOC and Ilhan Omar and now Abdul El-Sayed,” she added.

Barker’s warning comes as a new crop of progressive candidates and democratic socialists test its strength ahead of the midterm elections, including figures she says are carrying forward the movement that Sanders helped build.

Progressive Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, whom Barker specifically named as one of Sanders’ emerging “message bearers,” recently secured the Democratic nomination in a close primary against Rep. Haley Stevens.

Others have won key primaries elsewhere, including Mamdani-backed Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York.

Barker previously revealed to Fox News Digital that the Democratic Party’s leftward shift prompted her decision to leave the party, sharing that she was inspired to enter politics during former President Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign.

“If you look at him then, and you compare him to the modern movement of the party today, it is just night and day. They have gone left on so many critical issues, like immigration and identity politics, and defund the police and just all of these things that I did not sign up for,” she said.

She added that former President Joe Biden’s withdrawal from the 2024 presidential race and then-Vice President Kamala Harris’ subsequent nomination made her recognize in “real time the manifestation of everything the Democrats had become.”
